# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## What this is

A KiCad hardware project (schematic + PCB), not application code. It's a 3×3
macropad built around the Seeed XIAO ESP32-C6, with a rotary encoder and
per-key RGB, used to bring up two never-before-tested subsystems of the
[SMK](https://github.com/mburger89/SMK) firmware (the RMT LED driver and
`BatteryMonitor`) and the [SMK Configurator](https://github.com/mburger89/smk_configurator)
editor.

**The schematic and PCB are generated by Python scripts, not drawn by hand.**
`generate_test_board.py` is the source of truth and `router.py` generates
the copper; everything under `smk_test_board/` (`.kicad_sch`, `.kicad_pcb`,
`.kicad_pro`, `fp-lib-table`, `kbd.pretty/`) is generated output and must
never be hand-edited. Change the generator and re-run it instead. That
applies to tracks and pours exactly as it does to footprints: routing a
trace by hand in the KiCad GUI is undone by the next regeneration.

**Status: design complete, routed, DRC-clean, not yet fabricated.** Before
ordering, `docs/fabrication.md` opens with a STOP gate — two footprints
(`XIAO_ESP32C6_HEADERS`, `EC11_VERTICAL`) were hand-drawn from datasheet
dimensions and have never been checked against physical parts. That gate
is unrelated to routing and is still open.

## Required sibling repo

`generate_test_board.py` imports `generate_macropad.py` from
`~/esp/SMK_macro_pad` (hardcoded path, `sys.path.insert`) rather than forking
its s-expression/geometry helpers. The script raises `SystemExit` immediately
if that sibling isn't cloned next to this repo. Any change to shared
low-level helpers (footprint primitives, placement search, overlap checking)
belongs in that sibling, not here.

## Commands

```bash
python3 -m venv venv && venv/bin/pip install pytest   # one-time setup
venv/bin/python -m pytest                              # run all tests (28, ~1 min)
venv/bin/python -m pytest test_test_board.py::test_name  # a single test
python3 generate_test_board.py                          # regenerate (routes; ~60s)
python3 export_fab.py                                   # gerbers + drill + zip into gerbers/
```

DRC (via `kicad-cli`, not pytest):

```bash
kicad-cli pcb drc --refill-zones --output drc.rpt --severity-error smk_test_board/smk_test_board.kicad_pcb
kicad-cli pcb drc --refill-zones --output drc_full.rpt smk_test_board/smk_test_board.kicad_pcb   # + warnings
```

**`--refill-zones` is mandatory and `--save-board` is forbidden.** The GND
pours are stored as outlines only, so without the refill DRC checks two
empty zones and calls a board with no ground planes clean; with
`--save-board` KiCad writes its computed fill into the generated file and
breaks byte-reproducibility. Expected: **16 errors / 0 unconnected**
(errors-only), **99 / 0** with warnings. Neither routing nor the shrink to
65.7 × 91.73 mm added a DRC category — the unrouted 76 × 113.16 mm board
scored the same 16 errors, and the three-warning drop to 99 is the
silkscreen title moving to the bottom margin.

**Regeneration must be byte-reproducible, UUIDs included.** After any change
to the generator, run it and check `git diff` on `smk_test_board/` — it
should show exactly what moved electrically. If a documentation-only change
moves the `.kicad_pcb`, that's a real finding, not noise. `gerbers/` and
`*.zip` are gitignored; generate fresh at order time rather than trusting a
checked-in copy.

## Architecture of the generator

The generator is organized as five layers, in this order — the first four
in `generate_test_board.py`, the fifth in its own module:

1. **`PIN`** — the GPIO map. This is a cross-repo contract (see below); treat
   it as frozen unless deliberately renegotiating the pinout everywhere at
   once.
2. **`build_nets()`** — the netlist, as `net name -> [(ref, logical_pad), ...]`
   using logical pad names (`"A"`/`"K"` for diodes, `"VDD"`/`"DIN"` for LEDs,
   etc.), translated to real footprint pad numbers via `PAD_MAP` at the
   schematic/PCB emission boundary. This is the single source of truth for
   what connects to what — `build_sch()` and `build_pcb()` both read it
   rather than wiring anything independently.
3. **`build_sch()`** — emits the `.kicad_sch` text. Iterates `build_nets()`
   and `AUX_PARTS` to place symbols and wire/label them; `AUX_PARTS` exists
   specifically so a part with no hand-written schematic block still gets
   auto-placed — parts that skip both a hand-written block and this registry
   silently vanish from the schematic (this bit the project once: 12 real
   parts existed on the PCB but not the schematic until this registry was
   added).
4. **`build_pcb()`** — emits the `.kicad_pcb` text. Placement is
   obstacle-aware, not hand-coordinated: helpers like `_pad_obstacles()`,
   `_best_clear_offset()`, and `_cap_offsets_near()` read each neighboring
   footprint's *actual emitted geometry* (probed via a throwaway build with
   the UUID counter snapshotted/restored) and grid-search for a clear spot,
   rather than using hand-copied coordinates that silently go stale when a
   neighboring footprint changes.

   The **board outline is derived from that placement**, not chosen:
   `BOARD_W/BOARD_H = max extent + 5mm MARGIN`, from a fixed (0, 0) origin.
   So the right and bottom margins are always MARGIN, but the top and left
   ones are whatever `KEY_X0`/`KEY_Y0` leave over — which is why an
   assertion, not a comment, now checks that no footprint sits inside the
   near margin (a part placed up there hangs off the edge instead of
   widening the board, and `max()` alone would never notice). To resize the
   board, move parts; never hand-set a dimension.
5. **`router.py`** — routes the copper, then `build_pcb()` emits it. Same
   read-the-real-geometry principle one level up: the router is handed
   `build_pcb()`'s own emitted footprint text and parses the pads, holes
   and milled windows back out of it, so a footprint that changes shape
   changes what the router avoids with nothing to update by hand. See
   below.

Routing takes about a minute, so `build_pcb(route=False)` skips it;
`placed()`, `check_overlaps()` and every placement-only test use that.
`main()` always routes.

## The router

`router.py` rasterises every obstacle onto a 0.2 mm grid inflated by
clearance, then routes with an 8-direction A\* that charges `TURN_COST` per
direction change and `VIA_COST` per layer change — smoothness is a cost
term, not a post-process, which is what keeps routes from staircasing.
Four things about it are load-bearing:

- **Work is ordered by connection, not by net.** Each net is reduced to an
  MST, all edges from all nets go into one list, and the list is routed
  shortest-edge-first. Ordering by whole nets cannot work here: VSYS's 4 mm
  hop from an LED's VDD pad to its own decoupling cap and its 40 mm spine
  run cannot both be "early".
- **GND is a pour, not a routed net** — one zone per copper layer, which is
  also what the EMC analyser's top finding (GP-002) asks for. But
  connectivity does **not** depend on the pour reaching pads: a dense
  2-layer board fragments the back pour badly (ten pieces here), and pads
  have been stranded in 1.9 mm² islands. Every GND pad instead gets a short
  stub to its own via onto the front plane, which comes out essentially
  intact.

  That tie is a stub to a *nearby* via, so it only works where the pour
  around that via is healthy — and **a placement can seal a pocket that no
  placement-time obstacle set can see**, because the walls are routed
  traces that do not exist yet when the search runs. On the shrunk board
  the VBAT divider sat west of U1's pad 1, inside the corner where ROW0,
  ROW1 and ROW2 all dive for the back layer within 4 mm and VSYS closes it
  from the south; those five traces enclosed R1/R2 in 13.6 mm² of private
  GND with no path to the plane — one `unconnected_items` zone-to-zone
  error. The fix is in the *seed*, not the search: put parts that need
  ground near an MCU's fan-in on the open side of it. `--refill-zones` DRC
  is what catches this; the placement scan cannot.
- **Zones ship unfilled** — outlines only, filled at DRC/export time. See
  the DRC note above.
- **No via in a pad, ever** — enforced by a dedicated mask
  (`_build_via_mask()`), so it is not something the search can express, and
  re-checked on the emitted board by `test_no_via_sits_in_a_pad`.

Two geometry facts were learned the hard way and are worth not
re-discovering. KiCad applies a **negated rotation** to footprints on
B.Cu (pad offsets are not mirrored) — getting this wrong swapped anode and
cathode on all nine diodes and shorted every ROW trace. And a pad's stored
angle is **absolute**, with the footprint's rotation already baked in;
adding them double-counts, which mis-sizes exactly those diodes.

Four footprints have no generator in the shared `generate_macropad.py` module
and are built inline near the bottom of the file: `_fp_sk6812mini_tb()`,
`_fp_xiao_headers()`, `_fp_ec11_vertical()`, `_fp_bat_pads()`. Each is meant
to reproduce the *equivalent geometry* (not byte-identical — different UUIDs,
`fp_rect` vs. four `fp_line`s) of the corresponding master in
`smk_test_board.pretty/`; `test_footprints.py`'s parity tests enforce this
per element-class (pads/silk/courtyard/fab/Edge.Cuts) so a dropped layer
fails loudly. This project has one live scar from that exact failure mode:
`_fp_sk6812mini_tb()` once silently dropped all `Edge.Cuts` primitives (the
milled light window a reverse-mount LED shines through), which would have
shipped nine LEDs sealed behind solid FR4.

## The cross-repo pin-map contract

`PIN` in `generate_test_board.py` must agree with three other repositories:
`~/esp/SMK`'s `Main.swift`/`Kconfig.projbuild` (firmware), `~/esp/smk_configurator`'s
`KeyboardDesign.smkTestBoard` (editor), and this repo's own `keymap.json`.
Changing a GPIO here without changing it in all four means a board that
scans the wrong pins.

Two things about this pinout are easy to get backwards and worth
double-checking against `test_test_board.py` before believing a change is
correct:

- **The encoder's push-switch occupies matrix position row 0 / col 2** —
  there is no `SW02`; `build_nets()`, the diode-direction logic, and the LED
  chain all special-case this position.
- **The LED chain is wired serpentine** (even rows col0→2, odd rows col2→0)
  to match the firmware's `ledChainIndex()`, not raster (`r*COLS+c+1`). On a
  3×3 those two formulas only disagree on row 1 — this shipped wrong and
  passed review more than once before `test_led_chain_order_matches_firmwares_serpentine_mapping`
  was added to check all nine positions.

## Test suite structure

- `test_test_board.py` — netlist correctness (diode direction, LED chain
  continuity/order, no floating single-member nets), placement geometry
  (everything inside the board outline, LEDs at the right offset), the
  cross-repo pin-map contract, and a routing section: no via in a pad,
  every track octilinear, JLCPCB minimums, every multi-pad net carrying
  copper, GND poured on both layers. The routing tests share one
  session-scoped fixture because routing is slow; keep them on it.
- `test_footprints.py` — footprint file integrity (parses, balanced parens,
  minimum pad counts, connector geometry) and the inline-re-render-vs-library-master
  parity checks described above.

A relevant DRC fact for anyone touching the SK6812MINI-E placement or the
project file: `.kicad_pro` sets `min_copper_edge_clearance` to 0.2 mm,
*below* the LED pads' real ~0.2467 mm clearance to their own light windows.
That's a relaxed rule chosen to keep DRC at zero errors, not evidence the
clearance is generous — see `docs/fabrication.md`'s DRC triage table before
assuming a clean DRC run means "no tight clearance exists" anywhere on this
board.

## Docs map

- `docs/fabrication.md` — BOM, JLCPCB order spec, full DRC triage history
  (what moved and why, category by category), and the pre-order checklist —
